summary: The workshop begins with introductions and logistics. Apoorva Joshi defines AI agents as systems using LLMs to reason, plan, and execute tasks with tools, distinguishing them from simple prompting and RAG which lack iterative reasoning and personalization. Agents combine tools, memory, and iterative prompting for complex multi-step tasks. Planning patterns covered include Chain of Thought, Tree of Thoughts, ReAct, and Reflection. Memory is split into short-term (single conversation) and long-term (multiple conversations for personalization). Short-term memory may require condensation strategies like retrieving recent messages or summarizing. Long-term memory is largely unexplored; the emerging best practice is designing application-specific agents to narrow down tracked states. Tools are interfaces for agents to interact with the external world, defined as functions with descriptive names, detailed descriptions, and argument types, with modern LLMs trained to identify when functions should be called. The hands-on portion builds an AI research agent using Fireworks' free open-source firefunction V1 model, three tools (arXiv paper summaries, paper list retrieval, MongoDB knowledge base Q&A), and short-term memory persisted to MongoDB. Libraries introduced include datasets (HuggingFace arXiv embedding dataset), arxiv_loader (LangChain document loader), PyMongo, LangChain MongoDB/HuggingFace/Fireworks integrations, and LCEL with RunnableLambda. Agents are created using create_tool_calling_agent and create_react_agent constructors, executed via agent_executor, and given memory using runnable_with_message_history wrapping the agent runnable with MongoDB as the persistence backend. The workshop concludes with Apoorva requesting attendee feedback via a survey to improve future iterations and thanking the audience.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Workshop Overview
sections.summary: Apoorva Joshi introduces herself and the workshop structure: 20-30 minutes on concepts followed by hands-on agent building. Team members Tom, Ben, and Fabian assist. Links to slides and labs are shared via QR code and postcards.

sections.title: What Are AI Agents
sections.summary: Apoorva defines AI agents and contrasts them with simple prompting and RAG. Agents provide tools, memory, and iterative reasoning, enabling complex multi-step tasks, self-refinement, and personalization. Known challenges include long-term planning, cost, and latency.

sections.title: When to Use AI Agents - Examples
sections.summary: Interactive segment evaluating example tasks. Simple factual questions do not need agents. Company policy questions fit RAG. Tasks involving data aggregation, visualization, reasoning, and long-term personalization are good agent use cases.

sections.title: Planning and Reasoning Patterns
sections.summary: Covers planning without feedback (Chain of Thought, Tree of Thoughts) and planning with feedback (ReAct, Reflection). Chain of Thought prompts step-by-step thinking. Tree of Thoughts considers multiple paths with search. ReAct loops through thoughts, actions, and observations. Reflection uses critique loops.

sections.title: Agent Memory
sections.summary: Memory enables storing and recalling past conversations. Short-term memory handles single conversations; long-term memory spans multiple conversations for personalization. Short-term memory is straightforward unless conversations grow long, requiring condensation.

sections.title: Long-term Memory, Tools, and Research Agent Overview
sections.summary: Long-term memory is largely unexplored; best practice is designing application-specific agents to narrow tracked states. Tools are function interfaces for agents to interact with the external world, using descriptive names, detailed descriptions, and argument types. The research agent uses Fireworks firefunction V1, Chain of Thought and ReAct patterns, three tools (paper summaries, paper list, MongoDB Q&A), and short-term memory persisted to MongoDB.

sections.title: Hands-On Lab Logistics and Environment Setup
sections.summary: Apoorva explains lab navigation via QR codes, emoji indicators for hands-on sections, code block placeholders, and documentation references. First hands-on section covers MongoDB Atlas setup and dev environment configuration, allocated 15-20 minutes.

sections.title: Libraries, Tools, and Concepts for Hands-On
sections.summary: Introduces key libraries: datasets for downloading arXiv embeddings from HuggingFace, arxiv_loader for loading papers as LangChain documents, PyMongo for MongoDB, LangChain integrations (MongoDB, HuggingFace, Fireworks), and LCEL with RunnableLambda. Explains tool creation via LangChain tool decorator and the pipe operator for chaining runnables.

sections.title: Creating the Agent and Reasoning Patterns
sections.summary: Covers create_tool_calling_agent (prompt template with agent scratchpad, LLM with tool knowledge, output parser) and create_react_agent (ReAct prompt with stop sequences, thought/action/observation parsing). Agent executor is the runtime that calls the agent, executes actions, passes outputs back, and repeats until task completion.

sections.title: Adding Memory and Wrap-Up
sections.summary: Short-term memory is added by wrapping the agent runnable in runnable_with_message_history, which persists chat history to MongoDB organized by session ID. Apoorva requests feedback via a survey QR code, noting this is the first time running the workshop.

sections.title: Closing Remarks
sections.summary: Apoorva thanks attendees for participating and reiterates the request for feedback to improve future iterations of the workshop. The session concludes.
